title: Browser sessions and CSRF

richText: After form login, the server can store authentication in an HTTP session.
The browser holds a session cookie and sends it with later requests. The server uses it to find the session.
Logging out ends the application login. Secure cookies and HTTPS protect the cookie during normal use.
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) happens when another website causes the browser to send an unwanted request using credentials it sends automatically.
Session cookies are sent automatically. The unwanted request can therefore appear to come from a logged-in user.
Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default. Requests that change data normally need a CSRF token.
The application supplies this token in a form field or request header. Spring checks it before accepting the request.
GET requests should read data rather than change it. They normally do not need a CSRF token.
Choose settings from how credentials are sent
A stateless session policy does not, by itself, remove CSRF risk.
An API that accepts only bearer tokens explicitly added to the Authorization header can have different CSRF settings from a cookie-based application.
Before disabling CSRF, ensure the application does not also authenticate through cookies or browser-cached Basic credentials.
Keep CSRF protection when authenticated browser requests use a session cookie.

summary: Understand session cookies before choosing CSRF settings.
